newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end higher for 4th straight day.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end higher for 4th straight day.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries recovered from a shaky start to close higher for the fourth straight day on Thursday, helped by an afternoon bout of technical buying.

The 30-year bond closed at 104-11/32, up 13/32 from Wednesday, and just below its intraday high of 104-14/32. Its yield fell to 6.30 percent from 6.32 percent, its lowest level since mid-February, 1996.
"The technicals in the market are phenomenal," said Chris Fitzmaurice, a trader at Salomon Bros.
The afternoon buying spree followed a highly volatile morning, in which Treasury prices see-sawed up and down vigorously.
Bonds fell to session lows right off the bat, after the Labor Department reported a drop in jobless claims to 277,000 in the week ended July 26 -- well below the expected 306,000 level.
But the subsequent dips were bought, as the claims data were described as distorted by special factors and the digestion of the second-quarter gross domestic product report.
GDP rose at a 2.2 percent rate in the second quarter.

That was a bit above expectations, but the market cheered the downward revision to first quarter growth to a 4.9 percent pace from 5.9 percent, as well as a low 1.4 percent deflator in the second quarter -- implying low inflation.
Both retail and hedge fund accounts were said to have bought the dip at the long end, while central banks bought two-year notes, players said.
The gains, though, were short-lived, as the market used the second wave of economic data to take some profits.
The Conference Board's help wanted index soared 7 points in June, sparking fears of a strong July employment report.
Also, the Chicago purchasing managers's survey, while showing an overall decline in July, posted gains in prices and supplier deliveries.
"It was a nice place to take profits if you were long for a while," said Thomas Estes, head trader at SBC Warburg. "The market was way too high... but the market is still in good shape."
In addition to the profit taking, traders reported $2 billion sale of mortgages hit the Street, adding to the market's woes.
But once the market reached its lows, more buying on dips emerged, especially when the September T-bond hit 116-9/32. More technical buying occured at 116-16/32. The contract closed at 116-24/32.

Support for Treasuries also came from mortgage flows, a $1 billion Citibank asset backed deal which prompted STRIPS buying and defeasace buying from municipal bond refinancing, where Treasuries are bought to retain a AAA rating.
"There was a little something for everyone," Estes said.
Thursday's activity was rather heavy, with volume at about $100 billion, according to GovPX.
The market next faces a huge test in a duo of key economic data on Friday: the July employment report and the National Association of Purchasing Management's July manufacturing survey.

Traders said it would take very strong data and a clear acceleration of wage pressures to knock the market down. Some said a tame set of data would push the 10-year note below 6.0 percent and the 30-year bond to 6.25 percent.

In late trading, the two-year note was at 100-8/32, up 1/32, to yield 5.74 percent. The 10-year note was up 6/26 at 104-13/32 to yield 6.02 percent and the five-year note was at 100-13/32, up 5/32, to yield 5.91 percent.
Bill rates were down flat to two basis points lower.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
